The final answer is in `final.py` and scores **89.0** on the search split, using **8 of the 24 scorer calls**. The reference scores about 1.0, so this is roughly 89× faster, and every scored run was valid. Its two earlier scorer runs gave 88.0 and 87.8. The scorer varies by about ±3% between runs of the same file.

I announced the default budget from the skill: about 15 minutes, keeping some calls in reserve. I stopped after about 8 minutes because the last four variants I built made no measurable difference on my local test harness. That is earlier than the skill asks for.

## Results

| | Search score | Held-out (local harness, seeds 3–4) |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | ~1.0 | 1× |
| First champion (c1) | 69.9 | 86× |
| **Final (c15)** | **89.0** (also 88.0, 87.8) | **110×** |

The real held-out instances are hidden, so the held-out column comes from instances my own generator made, using seeds I never tuned on. It ranked the candidates the same way the scorer did.

## Why it's faster
The reference compares every pair of records (n² comparisons). `final.py` keeps the exact same test (`5·|A∩B| ≥ 4·|A∪B|`) but only runs it on a small set of candidate pairs:

1. **Identical word sets are grouped first.** Every pair inside a group is reported directly, and the matching below works on distinct sets only.
2. **Small sets are skipped.** Two different sets of up to 3 words can never reach 80%, and a 4-word set can only match a 5-word set that contains it. So sets of 4 or fewer words are never searched, and only 4-word sets are indexed.
3. **Prefix filtering.** Words are ordered from rarest to most common across all records. Two sets that are at least 80% alike must share one of the rarest few words of the larger set (n − ⌈4n/5⌉ + 1 words). An index of each set's rarest few words (n − ⌈8n/9⌉ + 1) finds the candidates. Sets are processed from smallest to largest, and candidates of the wrong size are dropped. On my test data, about 700–1,500 candidates were checked to find 1,700 pairs.
4. **A cheaper word ranking.** Each word's rank is its count times the number of distinct words plus its position, which gives a unique order without sorting. This was the last measurable gain: 81–84 → 88–89.

It also passed 200 small random cases and these edge cases: empty and whitespace-only records, many identical records, records that share most of their common words, and records with heavy word overlap.

## Approaches tried

| Candidate | Change | Result |
|---|---|---|
| c1 | Prefix filter, words ranked by frequency | Scorer 69.9 |
| c3 | Alphabetical word order instead of frequency | Only 4× locally (frequency order matters) |
| c5 | Skip sets of 4 or fewer words | Scorer 84.4, then 81.4 |
| c7 | Group duplicates with Counter and comprehensions | About 7% slower locally |
| c8 | Drop the `collections` import (it costs ~1 ms) | Scorer 81.2 (tie) |
| c9 | Separate index per set size | Slightly slower |
| c11 | Remove words that appear in only one set | About 10% slower locally |
| c13 | Use `bisect` to keep only candidates of the right size | Scorer 83.0; 5% faster on long records only |
| **c15** | **c5 plus the cheaper ranking** | **Scorer 88.0, 87.8, 89.0 → final** |
| c16, c18 | Sort all sets in one pass; cheaper size check | Tie locally, not submitted |

What is left is mostly unavoidable: about 2 ms of the ~6.5 ms per input goes to splitting the text into words and building the sets.

Everything else, including the harness (`work/harness.py`, `work/gen.py`) and all candidates, is in `work/`. The scorer's own log of the 8 calls is `calls.log`.
